translations.text: These are the names of the sons of Israel who came to Egypt with Jacob. Each man came with his household.
Reuben and Simeon, Levi and Judah,
Issachar, Zebulun, and Benjamin,
Dan and Naphtali, Gad and Asher.
All the people descended from Jacob numbered seventy. Joseph was already in Egypt.
Joseph died, along with all his brothers and that entire generation.
The Israelites grew, had children, and multiplied. They became very, very strong, and the land was filled with them.
A new king arose over Egypt who did not know Joseph.
He said to his people, “Look, the Israelite people are more numerous and stronger than we are.
Come, let us deal shrewdly with them before they multiply. Otherwise, if war comes upon us, they too may join our enemies, fight against us, and drive us out of the land.”
They appointed cruel overseers over them to subject them to forced labor. They built storage cities for Pharaoh: Pithom and Rameses.
But the more they subjected them to forced labor, the more they multiplied and the stronger they became. The Egyptians were distressed because of the Israelites.
The Egyptians ruthlessly subjected the Israelites to forced labor.
They made their lives bitter with hard work in mortar and bricks and every kind of work in the fields. In all their forced labor, they treated them ruthlessly.
The king of Egypt spoke to the Hebrew midwives, one of whom was named Puah and the other Shiphrah.
He said to them, “When you help the Hebrew women give birth, watch when they kneel down. If the child is a boy, kill him; if it is a girl, let her live.”
But the midwives feared God and did not do as the king of Egypt had told them. They let the boys live.
The king of Egypt summoned the midwives and said to them, “Why have you done this and let the boys live?”
The midwives said to Pharaoh, “The Hebrew women are not like the Egyptian women. They are vigorous and give birth before the midwife comes to them.”
God treated the midwives well because they had done this. The people multiplied and became very strong.
Because the midwives feared God, he established households for them.
Pharaoh commanded all the people, saying, “Throw every newborn boy into the river, but let every girl live.”
A man from the house of Levi went and married a daughter of Levi.
The woman conceived and gave birth to a son. She saw that he was beautiful and hid him for three months.
When she could no longer hide him, she took a basket of rushes, coated it with bitumen and pitch, put the child in it, and placed it in the marsh by the riverbank.
His sister stood at a distance to find out what would happen to him.
Pharaoh’s daughter went down to bathe in the river, while her servant women walked along the riverbank. She saw the basket in the marsh and sent her servant women to get it.
She opened it and saw the child. The child was crying, and she felt sorry for him. She said, “This is one of the Hebrews’ children.”
His sister said to Pharaoh’s daughter, “Shall I go and call a nursing woman from among the Hebrew women to nurse this child for you?”
Pharaoh’s daughter said to her, “Go.” So the young woman went and called the child’s mother.
Pharaoh’s daughter said to her, “Take this child and nurse him for me, and I will pay you your wages.” So the woman took the child and nursed him.
The child grew, and she brought him to Pharaoh’s daughter. He became her son, and she named him Moses, because she said, “I drew him out of the water.”
In those days, when Moses had grown up, he went out to his fellow Israelites and saw their forced labor. He saw an Egyptian man beating a Hebrew man, one of his fellow Israelites.
He looked this way and that, and when he saw that no one was there, he killed the Egyptian and buried him in the sand.
He went out the next day and saw two Hebrew men fighting. He said to the one at fault, “Why are you hitting your companion?”
He said to him, “Who made you a ruler and judge over us? Do you intend to kill me as you killed that Egyptian yesterday?” Moses was afraid and said, “Surely the matter has become known.”
Pharaoh heard about this and tried to kill Moses. But Moses fled from Pharaoh and went to the land of Midian, where he sat down by a well.
The priest of Midian had seven daughters. They came and drew water and filled the troughs to water their father’s flock.
The shepherds came and drove them away, but Moses stood up and rescued them and watered their flock.
They came to their father Reuel, and he said to them, “Why have you finished watering so quickly today?”
They said to him, “An Egyptian man rescued us from the shepherds. He even drew water for us and watered our flock.”
He said to his daughters, “Where is he? Why did you leave the man behind? Go, invite him to eat a meal.”
Moses agreed to live with the man, and he gave him his daughter Zipporah as his wife.

She gave birth to a son, and he named him Gershon, because he said, “I have been a foreign resident in a foreign land.” She also gave birth to a second son for Moses, and he named him Eliezer, because “The God of my fathers has been my help and has rescued me from Pharaoh’s sword.”
After those many days, the king of Egypt died. The Israelites groaned under their harsh forced labor and prayed, and their cry because of their forced labor rose to God.
God heard their groaning, and God remembered his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
God saw the Israelites, and God knew.
Moses was tending the flock of his father-in-law Jethro, the priest of Midian. He led the flock into the wilderness and came to Horeb, the mountain of God.
The angel of the Lord appeared to him in a flame of fire from within a bush. He saw the bush with fire blazing in it, yet the bush was not burning up.
Moses said, “I will turn aside and look at this great sight, to see why the bush is not burning up.”
The Lord saw that he had turned aside to look, and God called to him from within the bush, saying, “Moses, Moses!” He said, “Here I am.”
He said to him, “Do not come any closer. Take your sandals off your feet, because the place where you are standing is holy.”
He said, “I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” Moses hid his face, because he was afraid to look at God.
The Lord said, “I have indeed seen the oppression of my people in Egypt, and I have heard their cry because of their oppressors, for I know their pain.

I have come down to rescue them from the power of the Egyptians and to bring them up from that land to a spacious and good land, a land flowing with milk and honey, to the land of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites.
Now the cry of the Israelites has reached me, and I have also seen the oppression with which the Egyptians oppress them.
Now come, I will send you to Pharaoh, and bring my people, the Israelites, out of Egypt.”
Moses said to God, “Who am I to go to Pharaoh and bring the people of Israel out of Egypt?”
God said to him, “I will be with you. This will be the sign that I have sent you: when you have brought the people out of Egypt, you will worship God on this mountain.”
Moses said to God, “Look, I will go to the Israelites and say to them, ‘The Lord, the God of your ancestors, has sent me to you.’ They will say to me, ‘What is his name?’ What should I tell them?”
God said to Moses, “I am who I am.” And he said, “This is what you must tell the Israelites: ‘I am has sent me to you.’”

God said further to Moses, “This is what you must tell the Israelites: ‘The Lord, the God of your ancestors, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you.’ This is my name forever, and this is how I am to be remembered throughout all generations.

Go, gather the elders of the Israelites and say to them, ‘The Lord, the God of your ancestors, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, appeared to me and said: I have certainly remembered you and what has been done to you in Egypt.

I have said that I will bring you up out of the oppression of the Egyptians to the land of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites, to a land flowing with milk and honey.’

They will listen to you. You and the elders of the Israelites will go to the king of Egypt and say to him, ‘The Lord, the God of the Hebrews, has appeared to us. Now let us go three days’ journey into the wilderness and offer sacrifices to the Lord our God.’
But I know that the king of Egypt will not let you go, not even by his mighty hand.
I will stretch out my hand and strike the Egyptians with all the wonders that I will perform among them. After that he will send you away.
I will give this people favor in the eyes of the Egyptians, and when you leave, you will not leave empty-handed.
Each woman is to ask her neighbor and the woman staying in her house for gold objects, silver objects, and clothing. Put them on your sons and daughters, and plunder the Egyptians.”
Moses answered, “Look, they will not believe me or listen to me, for they will say, ‘The Lord has not appeared to you.’”
The Lord said to him, “What is that in your hand?” He said, “A staff.”
He said, “Throw it on the ground.” He threw it on the ground, and it became a snake, and Moses ran away from it.
The Lord said to Moses, “Reach out your hand and take hold of its tail.” He reached out his hand and grasped it, and it became a staff in his hand.
“This is so that they may believe that the Lord, the God of their ancestors, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has appeared to you.”
The Lord said to him again, “Put your hand inside your robe.” He put his hand inside his robe and took it out, and there was his hand, leprous, white as snow.
The Lord said to him, “Put your hand back inside your clothing.” He put his hand back inside his clothing and brought it out, and it had become like the rest of his flesh.
“If they do not believe or listen to the message of the first sign, they will believe the message of the second sign.
If they do not believe these two signs or listen to you, take some water from the river and pour it on the dry ground. The water you take from the river will become blood on the dry ground.”

Moses said to the Lord, “I beg you, my Lord, I have never been an eloquent man—not yesterday, nor the day before, nor since you began speaking to your servant. For my speech is halting, and my tongue is slow.”
The Lord said to him, “Who made the human mouth? Who makes a person mute or deaf, sighted or blind? Is it not I, the Lord?
Now go, and I will be with your mouth and teach you what to say.
Moses said, “Please, my Lord, send someone else, whoever you will send.”

The LORD’s anger burned against Moses, and he said to him, “There is your brother Aaron the Levite. I know that he can indeed speak. He is also coming out to meet you. When he sees you, he will rejoice in his heart.”
“You will speak to him and put the words in his mouth. I will be with your mouth and with his mouth, and I will teach you both what to do.”
“He will speak to the people for you. He will be your interpreter, and you will be like God to him.”
“Take this staff in your hand, so that you may perform the signs with it.”
Moses returned to Jethro his father-in-law and said to him, “Let me go back to my brothers in Egypt and see whether they are still alive.” Jethro said to Moses, “Go in peace.”
The LORD said to Moses in Midian, “Go back to Egypt, because all the men who were seeking your life have died.”
Moses took his wife and his sons, put them on a donkey, and set out to return to Egypt. Moses took the staff of God in his hand.
The LORD said to Moses, “When you return to Egypt, see that you perform before Pharaoh all the wonders I have done through your hands. But I will harden his heart, and he will not let the people go.”
“Say to Pharaoh, ‘This is what the LORD says: Israel is my son, my firstborn.”
“‘I told you to let my son go so that he may serve me. If you are unwilling to let my son go, look, I will kill your son, your firstborn.’”
While Moses was on the road at a lodging place, the LORD met him and sought to kill Moses.
Zipporah took a flint and cut off her son’s foreskin. She took hold of his feet and said, “I have a bridegroom of blood.”
He left him alone. Then she said, “A bridegroom of blood,” referring to the circumcision.
The LORD said to Aaron, “Go into the wilderness to meet your brother Moses.” He went and met him at the mountain of God, at Horeb, and kissed him.
Moses told Aaron all the words of the LORD, who had sent him, and all the signs he had commanded him to perform.
Moses and Aaron went and gathered all the elders of the Israelites.
Aaron told them all the words that the LORD had spoken to Moses, and he performed the signs before the people.
The people believed. They heard that the LORD had remembered the Israelites and had seen their oppression. The people knelt and worshiped before the LORD.
Afterward, Moses and Aaron went in and said to Pharaoh, “This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: Let my people go, so that they may celebrate a festival for me in the wilderness.”
Pharaoh said, “Who is the LORD, that I should obey him and let Israel go? I do not know the LORD, and I will not let Israel go.”

They said, “The LORD, the God of the Hebrews, has appeared to us. Let us go a three-day journey into the wilderness and offer sacrifices to the LORD our God, so that he does not strike us with the sword or with death.”
The king of Egypt said to them, “Moses and Aaron, why are you keeping the people from their work? Go back to your forced labor!”
Pharaoh said to them, “Look, the people of the land are now numerous, and you are keeping them from their work.”
That day Pharaoh gave orders to the overseers of the people and their scribes, saying to them:
You must no longer give the people straw for making bricks, as you did yesterday and the day before. Let them go and gather straw for themselves.

Impose on them the same number of bricks they used to make yesterday and the day before. Do not reduce it, because they are idle. That is why they cry out and say, ‘Let us go and sacrifice to our God.’
Let the work weigh heavily on the men, so that they concentrate on it and pay no attention to empty words.
The people's taskmasters and foremen went out and told the people, ‘This is what Pharaoh says: I will not give you straw.
Go yourselves and get straw wherever you can find it. But none of your work will be reduced.’
So the people scattered throughout the land of Egypt to gather stubble for straw.
The taskmasters pressed them, saying, “Complete your work as you always did, as when straw was given to you.”
The Israelite foremen whom Pharaoh's taskmasters had put in charge of them were beaten and asked, ‘Why have you failed, both yesterday and today, to complete your quota of bricks as you did before?’
The Israelite foremen came and cried out before Pharaoh, saying, ‘Why are your servants being treated this way?
Your servants are given no straw, yet we are told, “Make bricks!” Look, your servants are being beaten, and you are doing wrong to your people.’
Pharaoh said to them, “You are idle, utterly idle! That is why you say, ‘Let us go and sacrifice to the Lord.’”
‘Now go and work. You will not be given straw, but you must deliver the full number of bricks.’
The foremen looked unfavorably on the Israelites and told them, ‘You must not reduce the number of your bricks. It must be the same as every day.’
As they left Pharaoh's presence, they met Moses and Aaron, who were standing there facing them.
They said to them, ‘May the Lord look upon you and judge! You have made us offensive in the eyes of Pharaoh and his servants, handing us over to the sword in their hands to destroy us.’
Moses returned to the Lord and said, ‘My Lord, why have you brought harm on this people? Why did you send me?
Ever since I came to Pharaoh to speak in your name, he has harmed this people, and you have not rescued your people at all.’
The Lord said to Moses, ‘Now you will see what I will do to Pharaoh. Because of a mighty hand he will send them away, and because of an uplifted arm he will drive them out of his land.’
The Lord spoke to Moses and said to him, ‘I am the Lord.
I appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as God Almighty, but I did not make the name “the Lord” known to them.
I also established my covenant with them to give them the land of Canaan, the land where they lived as foreigners.
I have also heard the groaning of the Israelites, whom the Egyptians are enslaving, and I have remembered my covenant.

Therefore, tell the Israelites: I am the Lord God. I will bring you out from the Egyptians' oppression and rescue you from their forced labor. I will redeem you with a mighty hand, an uplifted arm, and great acts of judgment.
I will take you as my people, and I will be your God. You will know that I am the Lord your God, who brings you out from the Egyptians' oppression.
I will bring you into the land that I raised my hand and swore to give to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. I will give it to you as an inheritance. I am the Lord.’
Moses told the Israelites this, but they did not listen to Moses because of their discouragement and harsh slavery.
The Lord spoke to Moses, saying:
Go and tell Pharaoh, king of Egypt, to send the Israelites out of his land.
Moses said to the Lord, “Look, the Israelites do not listen to me. How will Pharaoh listen to me, when my tongue stammers?”
The Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron and gave them instructions concerning the Israelites and Pharaoh king of Egypt, to bring the Israelites out of the land of Egypt.
These are the heads of their ancestral households. The sons of Reuben, Israel’s firstborn: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi. These are the clans of Reuben.
The sons of Simeon: Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar, and Shaul, the son of a Canaanite woman. These are the clans of Simeon.
These are the names of the sons of Levi according to their generations: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. Levi lived 137 years.
The sons of Gershon: Libni and Shimei, according to their clans.
The sons of Kohath: Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel. Kohath lived 133 years.
The sons of Merari: Mahli and Mushi. These are the clans of the Levites according to their generations.
Amram married Jochebed, his uncle’s daughter, and she bore him Aaron, Miriam, and Moses. Amram lived 137 years.
The sons of Izhar: Korah, Nepheg, and Zichri.
The sons of Uzziel: Mishael, Elzaphan, and Sithri.
Aaron married Elisheba, the daughter of Amminadab and sister of Nahshon. She bore Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar.
The sons of Korah: Assir, Elkanah, and Abiasaph [?]. These are the clans of Korah.
Eleazar, Aaron’s son, married one of the daughters of Putiel, and she bore him Phinehas. These are the heads of the clans of the Levites according to their generations.
These are Moses and Aaron, to whom the Lord said, “Bring the Israelites out of the land of Egypt, all their divisions.”
They were the ones who spoke to Pharaoh king of Egypt about bringing the Israelites out of Egypt—Moses and Aaron.
It happened on the day when the Lord spoke to Moses in the land of Egypt.
The Lord spoke to Moses and said to him, “I am the Lord. Tell Pharaoh king of Egypt everything I tell you.”
Moses said to the Lord, “My tongue stammers. How will Pharaoh listen to me?”
The Lord said to Moses, “See, I have made you a god to Pharaoh, and Aaron your brother will be your prophet.
You shall say everything I command you, and Aaron your brother shall speak to Pharaoh, so that he will send the Israelites out of his land.
I will harden Pharaoh’s heart and multiply my signs and wonders in the land of Egypt.
Pharaoh will not listen to you. I will lay my hand on Egypt and bring my divisions and my people, the Israelites, out of the land of Egypt through great acts of judgment.
The Egyptians will know that I am the Lord when I raise my hand against the Egyptians and bring the Israelites out from among them.”
Moses and Aaron did as the Lord commanded them; that is what they did.
Moses was eighty years old, and Aaron was eighty-three years old when they spoke to Pharaoh.
The Lord said to Moses and Aaron:
“If Pharaoh says to you, ‘Give me a sign,’ tell Aaron, ‘Take your staff and throw it down before Pharaoh, and it will become a serpent.’”
Moses and Aaron came to Pharaoh and did as the Lord had commanded them. Aaron threw down his staff before Pharaoh and his nobles, and it became a serpent.
Pharaoh summoned the wise men and sorcerers, and the sorcerers of Egypt did the same through their sorcery.
Each threw down his staff before Pharaoh, and they became serpents. But Aaron’s staff swallowed their staffs.
Pharaoh’s heart grew hard, and he did not let them go, as the Lord had said.
The Lord said to Moses, “Pharaoh’s heart has grown hard, and he is unwilling to let the people go.
Go to Pharaoh in the morning, when he goes out to the water. Stand on the riverbank to meet him, and take in your hand the staff that became a snake.
Say to him, ‘The Lord, the God of the Hebrews, sent me to you, saying: Let my people go so that they may worship me in the wilderness. But until now you have not listened.
This is what the Lord says: By this you will know that I am the Lord. I am about to strike the water in the river with the staff in my hand, and it will turn into blood.
The fish in the river will die, the river will stink, and the Egyptians will struggle to drink water from the river.’”

The Lord said to Moses, “Tell Aaron, ‘Take your staff and raise your hand over the waters of the Egyptians—over their rivers, their channels, their ponds, and their reservoirs—and they will become blood. There will be blood throughout the land of Egypt, even in wooden and stone containers.’”
Moses and Aaron did as the Lord had commanded them. Aaron raised his staff and struck the water in the river in the sight of Pharaoh and his servants, and all the water in the river became blood.
The fish in the river died, and the river stank. The Egyptians could not drink water from the river, and there was blood throughout the land of Egypt.
The sorcerers of Egypt did the same through their sorcery. Pharaoh’s heart grew stubborn, and he did not listen to them, as the Lord had said.
Pharaoh turned and went into his house, and he did not take even this to heart.
All the Egyptians dug around the river for drinking water, because they could not drink the river water.
Seven days passed after the Lord struck the river.
The Lord said to Moses, “Go to Pharaoh and tell him, ‘This is what the Lord says: Let my people go so that they may worship me.
If you are unwilling to let them go, I am about to strike your whole territory with frogs.

The river will swarm with frogs. They will come up and enter your house, your private room, your sleeping chamber, and your beds, and enter your servants’ houses, among your people, and into your ovens and kneading troughs.
The frogs will climb onto you and all your people.’”
The Lord said to Moses, “Tell your brother Aaron, ‘Raise your hand with your staff over the rivers, the reservoirs, and the ponds, and bring frogs up over the land of Egypt.’”
Aaron raised his hand over the waters of Egypt, and the frogs came up and covered the land of Egypt.
The sorcerers also did the same through their sorcery and brought frogs up over the land of Egypt.
Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron and said to them, “Pray before the Lord, so that he may remove the frogs from me and my people. Then I will let the people go so that they may sacrifice to the Lord.”
Moses said to Pharaoh, “Choose a time when I should pray for you, your servants, and your people, so that the frogs may be removed from you and your house.”
He said, “Tomorrow.” Moses said to him, “It will be as you say, so that you may know that there is no one like the LORD our God.”
“The frogs will leave you, your house, your servants, and your people. They will remain only in the river.”
Moses and Aaron left Pharaoh, and Moses prayed before the LORD concerning the frogs he had brought upon Pharaoh.
The Lord did as Moses had said, and the frogs died in the houses, the courtyards, and the fields.
They gathered them into heaps, and the land stank.
When Pharaoh saw that there was relief, he made his heart stubborn and did not listen to them, as the LORD had told Moses.
The LORD said to Moses, “Tell Aaron, ‘Raise your staff and strike the dust of the ground, so that it may become lice throughout the land of Egypt.’”
He did so. Aaron raised his hand with his staff and struck the dust of the ground, and lice came upon people and livestock. All the dust of the ground became lice throughout the land of Egypt.
The magicians also did the same with their magic, but they could not remove the lice. The lice remained on people and livestock.
The magicians said to Pharaoh, “This is the finger of God.” But Pharaoh’s heart became hard, and he did not listen to them, as the LORD had said.
The LORD said to Moses, “Rise early in the morning and stand before Pharaoh as he goes out to the water. Say to him, ‘This is what the LORD says: Let my people go so that they may serve me.’”

“‘If you are unwilling to let my people go, I will send swarms of pests of every kind upon you, your people, and your houses. The Egyptians’ houses will be filled with swarms, just like the ground on which they live.’”
“‘On that day I will set apart the land of Goshen, where my people live, so that there will be no swarms there, so that you may know that I am the LORD in the midst of the land.’”
“‘I will make a distinction between my people and your people. This sign will happen tomorrow.’”
The LORD did so. He brought heavy swarms into Pharaoh’s house and his servants’ houses and throughout the land of Egypt. The land was ruined because of the swarms.
Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron and said to them, “Go and offer sacrifices before the LORD your God here in the land.”

Moses said, “It would not be right to do that, because what we sacrifice to the LORD our God is an abomination to the Egyptians. If we sacrifice the things the Egyptians worship before their eyes, they will stone us.”
“We will go a three-day journey into the wilderness and sacrifice to the LORD our God as he tells us.”
Pharaoh said, “I will let you go and sacrifice to the LORD your God in the wilderness. Only do not go very far away. Pray for me too.”

Moses said to Pharaoh, “I am leaving you now, and I will pray before the LORD. Tomorrow the swarms will leave Pharaoh, his servants, and his people. Only Pharaoh must not act deceitfully again by refusing to let the people go and sacrifice to the LORD.”
Moses left Pharaoh and prayed before the LORD.
The LORD did as Moses had asked and removed the swarms from Pharaoh, his servants, and his people. Not even one remained.
But Pharaoh hardened his heart this time too and did not let the people go.
The LORD said to Moses, “Go to Pharaoh and say to him, ‘This is what the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, says: Let my people go so that they may serve me.’”
“‘If you are unwilling to let them go and are still holding them back by force,’”
Look, the hand of the Lord will strike your livestock in the open country—the horses, donkeys, camels, cattle, and flocks—with a very severe plague.
The Lord will distinguish between Israel's livestock and the Egyptians' livestock. Not even one of all the livestock belonging to the people of Israel will die.
The Lord set a time: tomorrow the Lord would do this in the land.
The Lord did this the next day, and all the Egyptians' livestock died. But not even one of the livestock belonging to the people of Israel died.
Pharaoh sent and found that not even one of Israel's livestock had died. But Pharaoh's heart grew hard, and he did not let the people go.
The Lord said to Moses and Aaron, “Take handfuls of ashes from a furnace, and let Moses scatter them toward the sky in Pharaoh's sight.
They will become dust throughout the land of Egypt and cause boils with swellings to spread among people and livestock throughout the land of Egypt.”
They took the furnace ashes and stood before Pharaoh. Moses scattered them toward the sky in Pharaoh's sight, and they became boils with swellings that broke out on people and livestock.
The magicians could not stand before Moses because of the boils that had spread among the magicians and throughout Egypt.
The Lord hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he did not listen to them, just as the Lord had told Moses.
The Lord said to Moses, “Rise early in the morning, stand before Pharaoh, and tell him, ‘This is what the Lord, the God of the Hebrews, says: Let my people go so that they may serve me.
For this time I am sending my plagues against your heart, against your servants, and against your people, so that you may know that there is no one like me in all the earth.
For now I am stretching out my hand and striking you and your people with a plague, and you will perish from the earth.
But I have kept you standing for this very reason: to show you my power and to have my name proclaimed throughout the earth.
Even now you are oppressing the people and are unwilling to let them go.
Tomorrow at this time I will bring very severe hail, unlike any that has fallen in Egypt from the day it was founded until now.

Now send and bring your livestock and everything you have in the open country into shelter. The hail will fall on every person and animal found in the open country that has not been brought indoors, and they will die.’”
Those among Pharaoh's servants who feared the Lord's word brought their servants and livestock indoors.
But those who did not take the Lord's word to heart left their servants and livestock in the fields.
The Lord said to Moses, “Raise your hand toward heaven, and there will be hail throughout the land of Egypt, on people and livestock and on all the plants in the fields in the land of Egypt.”
Moses raised his staff toward the sky, and the Lord sent thunder and hail, and fire swept over the ground. The Lord sent hail down on the land of Egypt.
The hail fell, and fire blazed amid the hail. It was very severe, unlike anything that had happened throughout the land of Egypt since it became a nation.
Throughout the land of Egypt, the hail struck everything in the open country, both people and livestock. The hail destroyed all the vegetation in the fields and broke all the trees in the fields.
Only in the land of Goshen, where the Israelites lived, did no hail fall.
Pharaoh sent for Moses and Aaron and said to them, “This time I have sinned. The Lord is righteous, and I and my people are wicked.
Pray before the Lord—and there is ample room before him—that God's thunder and the hail may cease. I will let you go, and you will not stay any longer.”
Moses said to him, “When I leave the city, I will spread out my hands to the Lord. The thunder will stop, and no more hail will fall, so that you may know that the earth belongs to the Lord.
But as for you and your servants, I know that you still do not fear the Lord God.”
The flax and barley were destroyed, because the barley had formed ears and the flax had formed bolls.
The wheat and the spelt were not destroyed, because they ripened late.
Moses left Pharaoh and went out of the city. He spread out his hands toward heaven to the Lord. The thunder and hail stopped, and the rain no longer fell on the earth.
When Pharaoh saw that the rain, hail, and thunder had stopped, he sinned again. Pharaoh’s heart and the hearts of his servants became hard.
Pharaoh’s heart became stubborn, and he did not let the Israelites go, just as the Lord had declared through Moses.
The Lord said to Moses, “Go to Pharaoh, for I have hardened his heart and the hearts of his servants so that I may perform these signs among them,
and so that you may tell your son and your grandson what I did in Egypt and the signs I performed among them, and you may know that I am the Lord.”
Moses and Aaron came to Pharaoh and said to him, “This is what the Lord, the God of the Hebrews, says: ‘How long will you refuse to fear me? Let my people go so that they may serve me.
If you refuse to let my people go, tomorrow I will bring locusts throughout your territory.
They will cover the surface of the earth, so that no one will be able to see the ground. They will eat the remainder of what the hail left you, and they will eat all the trees growing in your fields.

Your houses, the houses of your servants, and the houses of all the Egyptians will be filled with them—something neither your fathers nor your fathers’ fathers have seen from the day they came into being on the earth until today.’” Then they turned and left Pharaoh’s presence.
Pharaoh’s servants said to him, “How long will this be a snare to us? Let the men go so that they may serve the Lord their God. Do you still not realize that Egypt is ruined?”
Moses and Aaron were brought back to Pharaoh, and he said to them, “Go, serve the Lord your God. But who exactly is going?”
Moses said to him, “We will go with our young and our old, with our sons and our daughters. We will go with our flocks and our herds, because we have a festival to the Lord.”
He said to them, “May the Lord indeed be with you if I let you and your households go! But beware, lest evil be ahead of you.
Not so! Go now, you men, and serve the Lord, since it is rest that you are seeking.” And they were driven out of Pharaoh’s presence.
The Lord said to Moses, “Raise your hand over the land of Egypt for the locusts, so that they may come up over the land of Egypt and eat the vegetation of the land and everything the hail has left.”
Moses raised his staff over the land of Egypt, and the Lord brought a hot wind over the land all that day and all that night. Morning came, and the hot wind carried in the locusts.

The locusts came up over the whole land of Egypt and settled throughout the Egyptians’ territory. They were extremely numerous. There had never been locusts like them before, nor would there ever be any like them afterward.

They covered the surface of the whole land, and the land became dark. They ate all the vegetation of the land and all the fruit of the trees that the hail had left. Not a leaf remained on a tree, nor any vegetation in the fields, throughout the land of Egypt.
Pharaoh hurried to summon Moses and Aaron and said to them, “I have sinned against the Lord your God and against you.
Now forgive my offense this once, and pray to the Lord your God that he may remove this death from me.”
Moses left Pharaoh’s presence and prayed to the Lord.
The Lord changed the wind and brought a very strong west wind. It carried away the locusts and cast them into the Red Sea. Not a single locust remained anywhere in the Egyptians’ territory.
The Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he did not let the Israelites go.
The Lord said to Moses, “Raise your hand toward heaven, and let there be darkness over the whole land of Egypt. Let the darkness grow thick.”
Moses raised his hand toward heaven, and there was darkness and gloom throughout the land of Egypt for three days.
No one could see anyone else, and no one rose from his place for three days. But all the Israelites had light where they lived.
Pharaoh summoned Moses and said to him, “Go, worship the Lord. Only leave your flocks and cattle behind. Your families may go with you too.”
Moses said to him, “You must also give us sacrifices and burnt offerings, so that we may sacrifice to the Lord our God.

Our livestock must also go with us. Not even a single hoof will be left behind here, because we must take some of them to worship the Lord our God. We will not know what we are to offer in worship to the Lord until we get there.”
The Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he was unwilling to send them away.
Pharaoh said to Moses, “Get away from me! Take care never to appear before me again, because on the day you appear before me, you will die.”
Moses said to him, “You have spoken well. I will never see your face again.”
The Lord said to Moses, “I am bringing one more plague upon Pharaoh and the Egyptians. Then I will send you away from here. When I have sent you away, all of you must leave this place.
Speak before the people: let each man ask his neighbor, and each woman her neighbor, for articles of silver and gold.”
The Lord made the Egyptians look favorably on the people. Moses himself was also very highly regarded in the land of Egypt, both by Pharaoh’s servants and by the people.
Moses said, “This is what the Lord says: ‘At midnight I will go out through Egypt.
All the firstborn in the land of Egypt will die, from the firstborn of Pharaoh, who sits on his throne, to the firstborn of the slave woman who is at the mill, and all the firstborn of the livestock.
There will be a great wailing in the land of Egypt, unlike anything that has happened before or will ever happen again.

But against the household of Israel, not even a dog will growl with its tongue, against either people or livestock, so that you may know that the Lord makes a distinction between the Egyptians and the household of Israel.’

All these servants of yours will come down to me and bow before me, saying, ‘Leave, you and all these people who are with you!’ Then I will leave.” And Moses went out from Pharaoh’s presence in great anger.
The Lord said to Moses, “Pharaoh will not listen to you, so that I may multiply my wonders in the land of Egypt.”
Moses and Aaron performed these wonders before Pharaoh. But the Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he did not send the Israelites out of his land.
The Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt.
This month will be the beginning of the months for you. It will be the first of all the months of the year for you.
“Tell the whole congregation of the Israelites: On the tenth day of this month, each man must take a lamb for his household, a lamb for his father’s household.

If the household is too small to consume a lamb, he and his nearest neighbor must take one together, according to the number of people. You must count the people for the lamb according to how much each person eats.
Your lamb must be without blemish, a year-old male. You may take it from the lambs or the young goats.
You must keep it until the fourteenth day of this month. Then the whole assembled congregation of the Israelites must slaughter it at twilight.
They must take some of its blood and put it on both doorposts, on the thresholds, and on the houses in which they eat it.
They must eat the meat that night, roasted over fire. They must eat it with unleavened bread and bitter herbs.
Do not eat any of it raw or boiled in water, but roasted over fire, with its head, legs, and internal organs.
Do not leave any of it until morning. Whatever is left of it until morning you must burn in the fire.
This is how you must eat it: with your belts fastened, your sandals on your feet, and your staffs in your hands. Eat it hurriedly, because it is the LORD’s Passover.

I will pass through the land of Egypt this night, and all the firstborn in the land of Egypt will die, from humans to livestock. I will execute judgment on all the gods of the Egyptians. I am the LORD.
This blood will be a sign for you on the houses where you are. I will see the blood and pass over you, and no deadly destruction will come upon you when I kill in the land of Egypt.
This day will be a memorial for you. Celebrate it as a festival to the LORD, a festival throughout your generations. You must observe it as a law forever.

For seven days you must eat unleavened bread. From the first day, remove the yeast from your houses. For whoever eats leavened bread from your houses, from the first day through the seventh day, that person will perish from among Israel.
The first day must be proclaimed holy, and the seventh day must be proclaimed holy for you. No work may be done on them, except for preparing what each person eats. That alone may be done for you.
You must observe the unleavened bread, because on this very day I brought your armies out of the land of Egypt. You must observe this day throughout your generations as a law forever.
In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month in the evening, you must eat unleavened bread, until the evening of the twenty-first day of the month.
For seven days no leavened bread may be found in your houses. For whoever eats leavened bread, that person will perish from the congregation of Israel, whether native-born or a resident of the land.
You must not eat anything leavened. Wherever you live, you must eat unleavened bread.
Moses called all the elders of the Israelites and said to them, “Quickly take sheep for your families and slaughter the Passover sacrifice.

Take a bundle of hyssop and dip it in the lamb’s blood. Sprinkle the lintel and both doorposts with some of the blood in the vessel. None of you may go out through the door of his house until morning.

The LORD will pass through to strike the Egyptians. He will see the blood on the lintel and both doorposts, and the LORD will pass over the doors. He will not allow the destroyer to enter your houses and destroy.
You must keep this command and this law, for yourselves and your children forever.
When you enter the land that the LORD will give you, as he said, you must observe this service.
And when your children say to you, “What is this ceremony?”

You must tell them, ‘It is the sacrifice of the LORD’s Passover, because he passed over the houses of the Israelites in Egypt when he struck the Egyptians and rescued our households.’” Then the people bowed down and worshiped the LORD.
The Israelites went and did so. Just as the LORD had commanded Moses and Aaron, so they did.

At midnight the LORD killed all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh, who sat on his throne, to the firstborn of the captive in prison, and all the firstborn of the livestock.
Pharaoh got up in the night, along with all his servants and all the Egyptians. There was great wailing in the land of Egypt, because there was no house without someone dead in it.
Pharaoh called Moses and Aaron that night and said to them, “Get up and leave my people, both you and the Israelites. Go and worship before the LORD, as you said.
Take your flocks and your cattle too, as you said, and go. Bless me too.”
The Egyptians urgently pressed the people to leave the land, because they said, “We are all dying!”
The people took their dough before it had risen, with their kneading bowls wrapped in their cloths and carried on their shoulders.
The Israelites did as Moses had said. They asked the Egyptians for silver articles, gold articles, and clothing.
The Lord gave the people favor in the eyes of the Egyptians, who gave them what they asked for. So they plundered the Egyptians.
The Israelites journeyed from Rameses to Succoth, six hundred thousand men on foot, besides their dependents.
A large mixed multitude also went up with them, along with sheep, cattle, and a very great number of livestock.

They baked the dough they had brought out of Egypt into unleavened cakes, because it had not risen. For the Egyptians had driven them out, and they could not delay or even prepare provisions for themselves.
The time the Israelites lived in Egypt was four hundred and thirty years.
At the end of four hundred and thirty years, on that very day, all the Lord’s hosts went out from the land of Egypt.
It was a night kept for the Lord to bring them out of the land of Egypt. This very night was to be kept for the Lord by all the Israelites throughout their generations.
The Lord said to Moses and Aaron, “This is the law of the Passover: no foreigner may eat of it.
But any slave whom a man has bought with money may eat of it after you have circumcised him.
A temporary resident or a hired worker may not eat of it.
It must be eaten in one house. You must not take any of its meat outside the house, and you must not break any of its bones.
The whole congregation of Israel must observe it.

When a foreigner lives among you and wishes to celebrate the Passover to the Lord, once every male of his household has been circumcised, he may come forward to celebrate it. He shall be like a native of the land. But no uncircumcised person may eat of it.
There shall be one law for the natives and for the foreigners living among you.”
All the Israelites did just as the Lord had commanded Moses and Aaron; that is what they did.
On that very day, the Lord brought the Israelites out of the land of Egypt, all their hosts.
The Lord said to Moses.
“Consecrate to me every firstborn that opens the womb among the Israelites, both human and animal. They are mine.”

Moses said to the people, “Remember this day, on which you came out of Egypt, out of the house of slavery, because the Lord brought you out of there with a mighty hand. No leavened bread is to be eaten.
Today you are going out, in the month of blossoms.

When the Lord brings you into the land of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Hivites, Jebusites, and Perizzites, as he swore to your ancestors to give you—a land flowing with milk and honey—you must perform this observance in this same month.
For seven days you must eat unleavened bread, and on the seventh day there shall be a festival to the Lord.
You must eat unleavened bread for seven days. No leavened bread is to be seen among you anywhere within your borders.
On that day you must tell your children, ‘This is because of what my God did for me when I came out of Egypt.’
It shall be a sign on your hand and a reminder between your eyes, so that the Lord’s law may be in your mouth, because the Lord brought you out of Egypt with a mighty hand.
Keep this commandment and this law at its appointed time, year after year.”
When the Lord brings you into the land of the Canaanites, as he swore to you and your ancestors, and gives it to you,
you must set apart for the Lord every firstborn that opens the womb. Every male offspring of your livestock that opens the womb belongs to the Lord.
You must redeem every firstborn male of the livestock that opens the womb with a lamb. If you do not redeem it, you must kill it. You must redeem every human firstborn among your sons.
When your son asks you in the future, ‘What is this?’ you must tell him, ‘With a mighty hand the Lord brought us out of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.

When Pharaoh stubbornly refused to let us go, the Lord killed all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the human firstborn to the firstborn of the livestock. That is why I sacrifice to the Lord every male that opens the womb, but I redeem all the firstborn of my sons.’
It will be a sign on your hand and a reminder between your eyes, because with a mighty hand the Lord brought you out of Egypt.

When Pharaoh let the people go, God did not lead them by the road through the land of the Philistines, although it was near. For God said, ‘The people might become afraid when they see war and return to Egypt.’
God led the people by the wilderness road toward the Sea of Reeds. The Israelites went up from the land of Egypt armed.
Moses took Joseph’s bones with him, because Joseph had solemnly made the Israelites swear an oath, saying, ‘God will surely remember you. Take my bones up from here with you.’
They set out from Succoth and camped at Etham, on the edge of the wilderness.
The Lord went before them by day in a pillar of cloud to guide them along the way, and by night in a pillar of fire to give them light, so that they could travel by day and by night.
The pillar of cloud by day and the pillar of fire by night did not depart from before the people.
The Lord spoke with Moses and said to him:
Tell the people of Israel to turn back and camp at the mouth of the canal, between Migdol and the sea, in front of Baal-zephon. You are to camp opposite it, beside the sea.
‘Pharaoh will say about the Israelites, “They are strangers in the land. The wilderness has hemmed them in.”’

The Lord said to Moses, ‘I will harden Pharaoh’s heart, and he will pursue you. I will be glorified through Pharaoh and his entire army, and the Egyptians will know that I am the Lord.’ And they did so.
The king of Egypt was told that the people had gone away. Pharaoh and his servants changed their minds about the people and said, ‘What have we done, letting Israel go from our service?’
He prepared his chariots and took his people with him.
He took six hundred selected chariots and all the chariots of the Egyptians, with men on all of them.
The Lord hardened the heart of Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and he pursued the Israelites. The Israelites had gone out with a raised hand.

The Egyptians pursued them and caught up with them as they were camped by the sea—all Pharaoh’s horses, his chariots, his horsemen, and his army. They were camped at the mouth of the gorge, opposite Baal-zephon.
Pharaoh approached, and the Israelites looked up and saw the Egyptians coming after them. They were very afraid, and the Israelites prayed to the Lord.
They said to Moses, ‘Was it because there were no graves in Egypt that you brought us out to die in the wilderness? Why have you done this to us and brought us out of Egypt?
Is this not what we told you in Egypt: “Leave us alone so that we can serve the Egyptians”? It would have been better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in this wilderness.’
Moses said to the people, ‘Do not be afraid. Stand firm and see the deliverance that the Lord will bring about for you today. For the Egyptians you have seen today, you will never see again.
The Lord will fight for you, while you remain still.’ And Moses prayed to the Lord.
The Lord said to Moses, “Why are you praying before me? Tell the people of Israel to move on.”
“Lift up your staff, stretch out your hand over the sea, and divide it, so that the Israelites may enter the sea on dry ground.”
“Look, I am hardening the hearts of the Egyptians so that they will go in after them. I will gain glory through Pharaoh and his whole army, his chariots and his horsemen.”
“The Egyptians will know that I am the Lord when I gain glory through Pharaoh and his whole army, his chariots and his horsemen.”
The angel of the Lord, who was going ahead of Israel’s camp, moved away and went behind them. The pillar of cloud also moved from in front of them and stood behind them.

It came between the Egyptian camp and the camp of Israel. There was cloud and darkness all night, but it gave light to the Israelites all night. Neither camp approached the other throughout the night.
Moses raised his hand over the sea, and the Lord drove the sea back with a strong, hot wind all night. He turned the sea into dry ground, and the waters divided.
The Israelites entered the sea on dry ground, and the waters were like a wall for them on their right and on their left.
The Egyptians pursued them and went in after them into the sea—all Pharaoh’s horses, his chariots, and his horsemen.
During the morning watch, the Lord appeared to the Egyptian camp in the pillar of fire and cloud, and threw the Egyptian camp into confusion.
He bound the wheels of their chariots, and they drove them with difficulty. The Egyptians said, “Let us flee from the Israelites, because the Lord is fighting for them against Egypt.”
The Lord said to Moses, “Stretch out your hand over the sea, and the waters will return over the Egyptians, over their chariots and their horsemen.”
Moses raised his hand over the sea, and at daybreak the sea returned to its place. The Egyptians were fleeing toward it, and the Lord swept the Egyptians into the sea.
The waters returned and covered the chariots, the horsemen, and Pharaoh’s entire army that had gone into the sea after them. Not even one of them remained.
But the Israelites walked through the sea as on dry ground, and the waters were like a wall for them on their right and on their left.
That day the Lord saved Israel from the power of the Egyptians, and Israel saw the Egyptians lying dead on the seashore.
Israel saw the great power that the Lord had exercised against the Egyptians. The people feared the Lord and trusted in the Lord and in Moses his servant.
Then Moses and the Israelites sang this song of praise to the Lord, saying, “Let us praise the majestic Lord, who triumphed over the horses and hurled their riders into the sea.”
“Mighty and praiseworthy is Yah, the Lord, and he has become our savior. This is my God, and I will praise him, my father’s God, and I will exalt him.”
“The Lord is a mighty warrior, skilled in battle; the Lord is his name.”
“He threw Pharaoh’s chariots and his army into the sea, and the finest of his warriors sank in the Red Sea.”
“The depths covered them; they went down into the deep and sank like stones.”
“Your right hand, Lord, is glorious in power. Your right hand, Lord, shattered your enemies.”
“In the greatness of your might you overthrew those who hated you. You sent out your wrath, and it consumed them like stubble.”
“At the blast of your nostrils the waters piled up. The flowing waters stood like waterskins; the depths congealed in the heart of the sea.”
“The enemy said, ‘I will pursue, I will overtake, and I will divide the plunder. My soul will devour them. I will draw my sword, and my hand will destroy them.’”
You blew with your wind, and the sea covered them. They sank like lead in the mighty waters.
“Who is like you, Lord? Who is like you, glorious in holiness, awesome and praiseworthy, working wonders?”
You raised your right hand, and the earth swallowed them.
In your kindness you led this people whom you redeemed; in your strength you led them to your holy dwelling.
The peoples heard and trembled; fear seized the inhabitants of Philistia.
Then the chiefs of Edom were afraid; trembling seized the men of Moab. All the inhabitants of Canaan were shattered.
May fear and terror fall upon them. By the greatness of your arm, may they sink like stones, until your people pass through, Lord, until this people whom you redeemed pass through.
You will bring them in and plant them on the mountain of your inheritance, the place you made for your dwelling, Lord—your sanctuary, Lord. Establish it with your hands.
The Lord will reign forever and ever.
For Pharaoh’s horses, his chariots, and his horsemen went into the sea, and the Lord brought the waters of the sea back over them. But the Israelites walked on dry ground through the sea.
Miriam the prophetess, Aaron’s sister, took a hand drum in her hand, and all the women went out after her with hand drums and tambourines.
Miriam sang in response to them: “Praise the exalted Lord, who has triumphed over the horses and thrown their riders into the sea.”
Moses led the Israelites away from the Sea of Reeds, and they went out into the wilderness of Shur [?]. They traveled three days through the wilderness and found no water.
They came to Marah, but they could not drink the water from Marah because it was bitter. That is why he called that place Marah.
The people complained against Moses and said to him, “What shall we drink?”
Moses prayed before the Lord, and the Lord showed him a piece of wood. He threw it into the water, and the water became sweet. There he taught him laws and judgments, and there he tested him.

He said to him, “If you listen carefully to the voice of the Lord your God, do what is right in his sight, pay attention to his commandments, and keep all his statutes, I will not bring upon you any of the plagues that I brought upon the Egyptians, for I am the Lord, your healer.”
They came to Elim, where there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees, and they camped there beside the water.

They set out from Elim, and the whole assembly of the Israelites came to the wilderness of Sin, which lies between Elim and Sinai, on the fifteenth day of the second month after the Israelites left Egypt.
The whole assembly of the Israelites grumbled against Moses and Aaron in the wilderness.

The Israelites said to them, “We wish we had died by the Lord’s hand in the land of Egypt, when we sat beside the pots of meat and ate bread until we were full! But you have brought us out into this wilderness to destroy the whole assembly of the Israelites with hunger.”

The Lord said to Moses, “Look, I will rain bread from heaven for you. The people shall go out and gather each day’s food on that day, so that I may test them to see whether they will follow my laws or not.
On the sixth day, they shall prepare what they bring in, and it shall be twice as much as they gather each day.”
Moses and Aaron said to all the Israelites, “In the evening you will know that the Lord brought you out of Egypt.
In the morning you will see the glory of the Lord, because your grumbling has been heard before the Lord. And who are we, that you grumble against us?”

Moses said to them, “When the Lord gives you meat to eat in the evening and bread in the morning to fill you—for the Lord has heard the grumbling that you direct against him. And who are we? You are not grumbling against us, but against the Lord.”
Moses said to Aaron, “Tell the whole assembly of the Israelites, ‘Come before the Lord, for he has heard your grumbling.’”
When Aaron spoke to the whole congregation of the Israelites, they turned toward the wilderness, and there the glory of the Lord appeared in the cloud.
The Lord said to Moses:
“I have heard the grumbling of the Israelites. Tell them, ‘At sunset you will eat meat, and in the morning you will have your fill of bread. Then you will know that I am the Lord your God.’”
In the evening, quail came up and covered the camp, and in the morning there was a layer of dew around the camp.
The mist of dew lifted, and there on the surface of the wilderness was a thin, flaky substance, crusted like ice on the ground.
The Israelites saw it and said to one another, “What is it?” For they did not know what it was. Moses said to them, “This is the bread that the Lord has given you to eat.”

“This is what the Lord has commanded: Gather some of it, each person as much as he needs to eat, one measure per person, according to the number of people you have. Each of you is to take some for those in his tent.”
The Israelites did so and gathered it, some gathering much and others little.
They measured it with the measure, and whoever had gathered much had nothing left over, while whoever had gathered little had no shortage. Each had gathered as much as he needed to eat.
Moses said to them, “No one is to leave any of it until morning.”
But they did not listen to Moses. Some men left some of it until morning, and it became infested with worms and stank. Moses was angry with them.
They gathered it every morning, each person as much as he could eat. When the sun grew hot, it melted.
On the sixth day they gathered twice as much bread, two measures for each person. All the elders of the congregation came and told Moses.

Moses said to them, “This is what the Lord has said: Tomorrow is a Sabbath of rest, holy to the Lord. Bake what you want to bake, and cook what you want to cook. Keep whatever is left over cool for yourselves until morning.”
They left some of it until morning, as Moses had commanded them, and it did not spoil, nor were there worms in it.
Moses said to them, "Eat it today, because today is a Sabbath to the Lord. Today you will not find it in the field."
“You are to gather it for six days, but the seventh day is the Sabbath. There will be none on it.”
On the seventh day some of the people went out to gather it, but they found none.
The Lord said to Moses, “How long will you refuse to keep my commandments and my laws?”

“See, the Lord has given you the Sabbath. That is why the Lord gives you bread for two days on the sixth day. Each of you is to stay where he is. No one is to go out through the door of his house on the seventh day.”
So the people rested on the seventh day.
The Israelites called it manna. It was white, like coriander seed, and tasted like a honey cake.

Moses said, “This is what the Lord has commanded: A full measure of it is to be kept for your future generations, so that they may see the bread I fed you in the wilderness when I brought you out of Egypt.”
Moses said to Aaron, “Take a jar, put a full measure of manna in it, and place it before the Lord to be kept for your future generations.”
Just as the Lord commanded me, Aaron placed it before the testimony to be kept.
The Israelites ate manna for forty years, until they reached an inhabited land. They ate manna until they reached the border of the land of Canaan.
The measure was one-tenth of a seah.
The whole congregation of the Israelites set out from the wilderness of Sin, traveling in stages at the Lord’s command. They camped at Rephidim, but there was no water for the people to drink.
The people quarreled with Moses and said to him, “Give us water to drink.” Moses said to them, “Why are you quarreling with me? Why are you putting the Lord to the test?”
The people were thirsty for water there, and they grumbled against Moses and said to him, “Why did you bring us up out of Egypt—to kill us, our children, and our livestock with thirst?”
Moses prayed before the Lord and said, “What am I to do with these people? They are almost ready to stone me.”
The Lord said to Moses, “Go ahead of the people and take some of the elders of Israel with you. Take in your hand the staff with which you struck the river, and go.”
“Look, I will stand there before you on the rock at Horeb. Strike the rock, and water will come out of it for the people to drink.” Moses did so in the sight of the elders of the Israelites.
He named that place Massah and Meribah because the Israelites quarreled and because they put the Lord to the test, saying, “Is the Lord among us or not?”
Amalek came to fight against Israel at Rephidim.
Moses said to Joshua, “Choose men for yourself and go out. Tomorrow let us fight against Amalek. I will stand on top of the hill with the staff of God in my hand.”
Joshua did as Moses told him and went to fight against Amalek. Moses, Aaron, and Hur went up to the top of the hill.
Whenever Moses raised his hands, Israel prevailed, and whenever he lowered his hands, Amalek prevailed.
Moses’ hands grew tired. They took a stone and placed it under him, and he sat on it. Aaron and Hur supported his hands, one on either side, so that his hands remained steady until sunset.
Joshua defeated Amalek and his people with the edge of the sword.
The Lord said to Moses, “Write this as a memorial in a book and set it before Joshua son of Nun, because I will completely erase the memory of Amalek from under heaven.”
Moses built an altar and named it “The Lord Is My Banner.”
He said, “Look, a hand is upon the throne! The Lord is at war with Amalek from generation to generation.”
Jethro, the priest of Midian and Moses’ father-in-law, heard about everything God had done for Moses and for Israel his people, and how the Lord had brought the Israelites out of Egypt.
Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, took his daughter Zipporah, Moses’ wife, after Moses had sent her away,
and her two sons. One was named Gershom, because Moses had said, “I have been a foreign resident in a foreign land.”
The other was named Eliezer, because “The God of my fathers has been my help and has rescued me from Pharaoh’s sword.”
Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, came to Moses with Moses’ sons and wife, into the wilderness where he was camped, at the mountain of God.
Moses was told, “Your father-in-law Jethro is coming to you, with your wife and your two sons.”
Moses went out to meet his father-in-law, bowed down to him, and kissed him. They asked about each other’s well-being and went into the tent.

Moses told his father-in-law everything the Lord had done to Pharaoh and the Egyptians for the sake of the Israelites, and about all the hardships they had suffered on the way and how the Lord had rescued them.
Jethro rejoiced over all the good things the Lord had done for Israel, rescuing them from the power of the Egyptians and from the power of Pharaoh.
Jethro said, “Blessed be the Lord, who has rescued you from the power of the Egyptians and from the power of Pharaoh, and who has rescued his people from under the Egyptians’ control.
Now I know that the Lord is greater than all the gods, because of what they plotted against them.”
Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, offered whole burnt offerings and sacrifices to the Lord. Aaron and all the elders of the Israelites came to eat a meal with Moses’ father-in-law before God.
The next day Moses sat down to judge the people, and the people stood around Moses from morning until evening.

Moses’ father-in-law saw everything he was doing for the people and said to him, “What is this you are doing for the people? Why do you sit alone while all the people stand around you from morning until evening?”
Moses said to his father-in-law, “The people come to me to ask for guidance from God.
Whenever they have a dispute, they come to me, and I judge between one person and another and make known to them God’s commandments and laws.”
Moses’ father-in-law said to him, “What you are doing is not good.
You will surely wear yourself out, both you and all these people with you, because this task is too heavy for you. You cannot do it alone.
Now listen to me, and I will advise you, and may God be with you. Be a teacher to the people on God’s behalf, and bring their cases before God.
Instruct them to keep the commandments and laws. Show them the way they should follow and the things they should do.

Select capable men from all the people, men who fear God, trustworthy men who hate bribery and deceit. Appoint them over the people as leaders of thousands, leaders of hundreds, leaders of fifties, and leaders of tens.
Let them judge the people at all times. When there is a major case, let them come to you, but let them judge every minor case themselves. Lighten your burden, and let them carry it with you.
If you do this, and God commands you, you will be able to endure, and all these people will go home in peace.”
Moses listened to his father-in-law and did everything he told him.
Moses chose capable men from all Israel and appointed them as leaders over the people: leaders of thousands, leaders of hundreds, leaders of fifties, and leaders of tens.
They judged the people at all times. They brought difficult cases to Moses, but they judged minor cases themselves.
Moses sent his father-in-law on his way, and he went to his own land.
In the third month after the Israelites came out of Egypt, on that very day, they came to the wilderness of Sin.
They set out from Rephidim and came to the wilderness of Sinai. They camped in the wilderness, and Israel camped there opposite the mountain.
Moses went up to God, and God called to him from the mountain and said, “This is what you must say to the house of Jacob and tell the Israelites:
‘You have seen what I did to the Egyptians, and how I carried you as though on eagles’ wings and brought you to myself.
Now, if you truly obey my voice and keep my covenant, you will be dearer to me than all the peoples of the earth, for the earth is mine.
You will be a kingdom, priests, and a holy nation for me.’ These are the words you must say to the house of Israel.”
Moses came and called the elders of the people and set before them all these words that the Lord had commanded him.
All the people answered together, “We will do everything the Lord has said.” Moses brought the people’s words back to the Lord.

The Lord said to Moses, “Look, I am coming to you in a thick cloud, so that the people may hear when I speak with you and may also trust you forever.” Moses reported the people’s words before the Lord.
The Lord said to Moses, “Go to the people and consecrate them today and tomorrow, and let them wash their clothes.
Let them be ready for the third day, because on the third day the Lord will come down onto Mount Sinai in the sight of all the people.
Give the people a solemn warning and say to them, ‘Be careful not to go up the mountain or approach its foot. Whoever approaches the mountain must be put to death.
No hand may touch that person, but they must certainly be stoned or shot. Whether animal or human, they must not live.’ When the horn falls silent, you are permitted to go up the mountain.”
Moses went down from the mountain to the people. He consecrated the people, and they washed their clothes.
He said to the people, “Be ready for the third day. Do not have sexual relations with a woman.”
On the third day, when morning came, there was thunder and lightning, and a dense cloud lay over the mountain. The sound of the horn was very loud, and all the people in the camp trembled.
Moses brought the people out of the camp to meet God, and they stood at the foot of the mountain.
Mount Sinai was entirely covered in smoke because the Lord had descended on it in fire. Its smoke rose like smoke from a furnace, and the whole mountain shook violently.
The sound of the horn grew louder and louder. Moses spoke, and God answered him with a voice.
The Lord descended onto Mount Sinai, to the top of the mountain. The Lord called Moses to the top of the mountain, and Moses went up.
The Lord said to Moses, "Go down and warn the people not to go too far before the Lord to see him, lest many of them fall."
The priests who approach the Lord must also consecrate themselves, so that the Lord does not strike them.
Moses said to the Lord, “The people cannot come up Mount Sinai, because you yourself warned us and told me, ‘Set a boundary around the mountain and consecrate it.’”
The Lord said to him, “Go down, then come up with your brother Aaron. But the priests and the people must not venture up before the Lord, lest he kill some of them.”
Moses went down to the people and spoke to them.
God spoke all these words:
“I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.
You must have no other gods besides me.
You must not make for yourself any image or any likeness of anything in heaven above, on the earth below, or in the waters beneath the earth.

You must not bow down to them or serve them, because I, the Lord your God, am a jealous God, bringing punishment for the fathers’ sins upon their children to the third and fourth generations of those who hate me.
But I show kindness to thousands of generations of those who love me and keep my commandments.
You must not swear falsely by the name of the Lord your God, because the Lord will not acquit anyone who swears falsely by his name.
Remember the Sabbath day and keep it holy.
For six days you shall labor and do all your work.

But the seventh day is a Sabbath to the Lord your God. You must not do any work—you, your son, your daughter, your male slave, your female slave, your livestock, or the foreigner residing in your towns.
For in six days the Lord made heaven and earth, the seas, and everything in them, and he rested on the seventh day. Therefore the Lord blessed the seventh day and made it holy.
Honor your father and your mother, so that your days may be many in the land that the Lord your God is giving you.
You must not kill.
You must not commit adultery.
You must not steal.
You must not give false testimony against your neighbor.
You must not covet your neighbor’s house. You must not covet your neighbor’s wife, his male slave, his female slave, his ox, his donkey, or anything that belongs to your neighbor.”
All the people saw the thunder and the flashes of lightning, the sound of the horn, and the smoking mountain. The people saw and were afraid, and they stood at a distance.
They said to Moses, “You speak to us, and we will listen. But do not let God speak to us, or we will die.”
Moses said to the people, “Do not be afraid, for God has come to test you, so that the fear of him may remain before you and you may not sin.”
The people stood at a distance, while Moses approached the thick darkness where God was.
The Lord said to Moses, “This is what you must say to the house of Israel: ‘You yourselves have seen that I have spoken to you from heaven.
You must not make gods of gold for yourselves alongside me, nor must you make gods of silver for yourselves.
Make an altar of earth for me, and sacrifice on it your burnt offerings and your offerings, your sheep and your cattle. In every place where you remember my name, I will come to you and bless you.
If you make an altar of stone for me, do not build it with cut stones, for by raising iron over it you defile it.
Do not go up to my altar by steps, so that your nakedness is not exposed on it.’
“These are the laws that you must set before them.
When you buy a Jewish slave, he must serve you for six years, and in the seventh he must leave you as a free man.
If he comes in alone, he must leave alone. If he is married, his wife must leave with him.
If his master gives him a wife and she bears him sons and daughters, the wife and her children will belong to his master, and he must leave alone.
But if the slave says, ‘I love my master, my wife, and my children; I will not go free,’
his master must bring him before the judges and bring him to the door or the threshold. His master must pierce his ear with an awl, and he will be his slave, serving him forever.
When a man sells his daughter as a female slave, she must not go free as male slaves do.
If she displeases her master, so that he does not marry her, he must let her be redeemed. He has no right to sell her to a foreign people, because he has dealt deceitfully with her.
If he takes her as a wife for his son, he must treat her according to the law for daughters.
If he takes another wife for himself, he must not reduce her food, her clothing, or her marital rights.
If he does not do these three things for her, she shall go free without any payment of money.
Anyone who strikes a man so that he dies must be put to death.
But if he did not lie in wait for him, and God delivered him into his hand, set aside a place for yourself where he may flee.
If a man acts brazenly against his neighbor and kills him by deceit, take him away even from my altar to put him to death.
Anyone who strikes his father or his mother must be put to death.
Anyone who kidnaps a person and sells him, and the person is found in his possession, must be put to death.
Anyone who reviles his father or his mother must be put to death.
When two men quarrel and one strikes the other with a stone or with his fist, and he does not die but becomes bedridden,
If he gets up and walks outside with his staff, the one who struck him shall be acquitted. He must only pay for his lost time and his medical treatment.
When a man strikes his male or female slave with a rod, and the slave dies under his hand, he must be punished.
But if he survives a day or two, the owner shall not be punished, because he is his property.

When two men fight and strike a pregnant woman, so that her child comes out, but no harm follows, the offender must pay a fine as the woman's husband demands of him. He shall pay as the judges determine.
But if harm follows, he shall give life for life.
An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth, a hand for a hand, a foot for a foot.
Burn for burn, wound for wound, bruise for bruise.
When a man strikes the eye of his male or female slave and destroys it, he shall set the slave free in compensation for the eye.
If he knocks out a tooth of his male or female slave, he shall set the slave free in compensation for the tooth.
When an ox gores a man or a woman to death, the ox must be stoned, and its meat must not be eaten. The owner of the ox shall be acquitted.

But if the ox had been in the habit of goring before, and its owner had been warned but had not kept it under control, and it kills a man or a woman, the ox shall be stoned, and its owner shall also be put to death.
If a payment is imposed on him, he shall pay whatever is demanded of him as a ransom for his life.
If an ox gores a son or a daughter, it shall be dealt with according to this judgment.
If an ox gores a male or female slave, its owner shall give thirty silver staters to the slave's master, and the ox shall be stoned.
When a man opens a pit, or a man digs a well and does not cover it, and an ox or a donkey falls into it,
the owner of the pit shall pay money to the animal's owner, and the dead animal shall belong to him.
When one man's ox gores another man's ox and it dies, they shall sell the living ox and divide its price. They shall also divide the dead animal.

But if it was known that the ox had been in the habit of goring before, and its owner had not kept it under control, he shall give an ox in compensation for the ox, and the dead animal shall belong to him.
When a man steals an ox or a sheep and slaughters or sells it, he shall give five oxen in compensation for the ox and four sheep in compensation for the sheep.
If a thief is caught breaking in and is struck and dies, there is no bloodguilt for killing him.
But if the sun has risen on him, there is bloodguilt for killing him. The thief must make restitution. If he has nothing, he shall be sold to pay for his theft.
If the stolen animal is found alive in his possession, whether an ox, a donkey, or a sheep, he shall repay double.

When a man lets livestock graze in a field or vineyard, and lets his livestock loose so that it grazes in someone else's field, he shall make restitution from the best of his own field and the best of his own vineyard.
When a fire breaks out and catches in thorns, and consumes stacked grain, standing grain, or a field, the one who started the fire must make restitution.
When a man gives his neighbor money or articles for safekeeping, and they are stolen from the man's house, if the thief is found, he shall repay double.
If the thief is not found, the owner of the house shall come before the judges to determine whether he has taken his neighbor's property.

In every case of wrongdoing involving an ox, a donkey, a sheep, clothing, or any lost property about which someone says, 'This is it,' the cases of both parties shall come before the judges. The one whom the judges find guilty shall repay his neighbor double.
When a man gives his neighbor a donkey, an ox, a sheep, or any livestock to keep, and it dies, is injured, or is carried off, with no one seeing it,
an oath by the Lord shall settle the matter between them, that he has not taken his neighbor's property. The owner shall accept the oath, and the keeper shall not make restitution.
But if it is stolen from him, he shall make restitution to its owner.
If it is torn apart, he shall bring it as evidence. He shall not make restitution for the torn animal.
When a man borrows an animal from his neighbor and it is injured or dies while its owner is not with it, he must make full restitution.
But if its owner is with it, he need not make restitution. If it is hired, the loss is covered by its hire.
When a man seduces a virgin who is not betrothed and sleeps with her, he must take her as his wife.
If her father is unwilling to give her to him, he must weigh out silver equal to the bride-price for virgins.
You must not let a sorcerer live.
Anyone who sleeps with an animal must be put to death.
Whoever sacrifices to gods other than the Lord alone must be destroyed.
You must not mistreat or oppress foreigners living among you, because you were foreigners in the land of Egypt.
You must not mistreat any widows or orphans.
If you mistreat them and they pray to me, I will certainly hear their prayer.
My anger will blaze up, and I will kill you with the sword. Your wives will become widows, and your children will become orphans.
If you lend money to someone among my people, to a poor person living with you, you must not act as a creditor toward him or charge him interest.
If you take your neighbor’s garment as a pledge, return it to him by sunset.
